NOTES

Coach: this deck has three parts. Part 1 is today's lesson. Part 2 is the homework slides. Part 3 is how we put it together. The survey results on slide 3 are shown without names on purpose.

WHAT EXCEEDS MEANS
Exceeds has no set words. The judge writes why.
The rubric has four levels: Beginning 1, Developing 2, Accomplished 3, Exceeds 4. For Exceeds, the judge must write a comment saying how we exceeded. So we need things a judge can write down.
1 Beginning
2 Developing
3 Accomplished
4 Exceeds
the judge writes why
1. Accomplished first
Every row needs the Accomplished words first. You can't skip a level.
2. Evidence to write down
A number we measured. A true story with before and after. A thing we can show, like an old attachment.
3. All five of us
The judges choose who answers. Any of us can explain any part, with our own examples.
NOTES

Ask: what is the difference between 'it works' and 'it worked 9 out of 10 times'? The second one is something a judge can write in the Exceeds box.

We know a lot. Some things only one of us knows.

SocketWhat is plugged in

QUICK FIX · 2 OF 4 MISSED A FACE QUESTION
face(90) points 90 degrees from where we started
Why it matters
face measures every turn from base, the way the robot pointed at the start. A small mistake in one turn is not passed on to the next.
 
Round a square: about 1 degree off with face. 17 degrees off without it.
NOTES

Check question: the robot is already pointing at 90. What does face(90) do? Answer: nothing, it is already there. A 'turn 90' would turn another quarter.

QUICK FIX · 2 OF 4 MISSED THIS
YAW_SIGN = -1 says which way the gyro counts
What it means
The gyro gives a number for which way the robot points. Ours counts UP when the robot turns anticlockwise. YAW_SIGN = -1 tells the code that, so it steers the right way.
How we found out (20 September)
drive_cm(-44) should have driven backwards. The robot spun on the spot instead, because the code was steering the wrong way. We flipped the sign, and it drove straight.
 
That is an ITERATE story.
NOTES

Not 'the robot drives backwards', not 'the motor is plugged in backwards', not 'how fast it turns'. Those were the wrong answers picked.

CREATE GAP · NO ONE MENTIONED THIS
The BOXOR frame and gravity mounting
Say it
"We started from a published design, the BOXOR frame. Its bevel gears turn the motor's movement round a corner to swing an arm. Attachments sit on pegs, held by their own weight, so a swap is one move."
NOTES

The rubric says 'original designs OR improved on existing ones'. So never say 'we invented it'. Say what we changed. Good examples from the test: one arm became two arms for missions 1 and 2. The mission 2 attachment with a circle kept getting stuck, so we changed it.

CREATE · WHY PYTHON
We code in Python. Here's why.
Last year's code
Last season's team left us tuned Python, with drive_cm in it. We only changed the wheel size.
More control
We choose every number, write our own commands, and do maths like the gyro correction.
Write it once
drive_cm and face live in our library. Every run uses them, so one fix helps every run.
See every change
git shows exactly which line changed and when. Every #was note is a test.
Test without the robot
A pretend robot in the browser, and 34 automatic checks in a few seconds.
It found bugs
Turning the blocks library into Python found 11 bugs, like pi written as 3.146.
NOTES

We started the season in Word Blocks, then moved to Python. Say it fairly: blocks are a good way to start. Python gave us more control and let us test and track every change. The 11 bugs: 8 found by reading the blocks, 3 more by testing on the robot.

CREATE · HOW DRIVE_CM WORKS
drive_cm: last year's command, our wheels
FROM LAST YEAR
drive_cm came from last season's Python. Our wheels are smaller, so we changed one number.
Wheel size30 cm is
Last year88 mm391 wheel degrees
Our robot62.4 mm551 wheel degrees
WHEEL_D_MM = 62.4
set_calibration_scale(179/180)
We asked for 180 cm and got 179, so the second line fixes every distance.
1
Centimetres to wheel degrees
One wheel turn is pi x 62.4 mm = 196 mm. So 30 cm is 551 degrees of wheel turn.
2
Pick a speed
Under 30 cm it goes slower. drive_cm(-30) goes backwards.
3
Ramp up and down
Speed up gently, hold, slow down gently, so the wheels don't slip.
4
Steer with the gyro
Every 15 ms it checks the gyro and steers back to straight. Next slide.
5
Brake a little early
The robot rolls on after braking, so it brakes about 1.4 cm early.
NOTES

Last year's toolKit.py is in code/2025-reference/Library/. It had drive_cm and set_calibration_scale already, with WHEEL_D_MM = 88.0. Our robot has 62.4 mm wheels, so we changed that one number. The distance maths is the same: centimetres, then wheel turns, then degrees. Say it to a judge: 'We kept last year's drive command and measured our own robot to fit it.' The safety stop: it refuses any distance longer than the mat, 200 cm.

CREATE · THE GYRO CORRECTION ALGORITHM
How the gyro keeps us driving straight
The full version, with the safety stops, is the drive_cm flowchart on How Our Code Is Designed.
1
Read the gyro
How far are we off straight? That is the error, in degrees.
2
Work out the steer
trim = -(18.9 x error + 5.25 x how fast the error changes)
3
Steer
Left wheel: speed + trim. Right wheel: speed - trim.
4
Wait and repeat
Wait 15 ms and go round again: about 66 times a second.
Example: the robot drifts 5 degrees left, so the error is -5. trim = -(18.9 x -5) = +94. The left wheel speeds up by 94 and the right slows by 94, so it steers back right. More than 45 degrees off: it stops.
NOTES

This is in code/library/advanced.py, lines 446 to 460. The first part steers harder the further off we are. The second part, 5.25 x the change, calms the steering so the robot doesn't wiggle. The minus sign makes it steer against the mistake: without it, the robot spirals. The pretend robot in code/learn/gyro-correction.html shows it moving.

Two answers that don't match
Colour sensors: settled
One of us wrote that we never used colour sensors. Our notes say we stopped using them on 20 September.
 
The agreed answer: two colour sensors are plugged into the hub, but only the gyroscope steers.
 
• Why the gyroscope? It works everywhere on the mat, not only near a line.
How many missions
One answer said 11 missions. Our final programs show fewer runs.
 
• Count them on the missions table.

ITERATE GAP · THE WEAKEST ROW IN THE TEST
A fix story has four parts
PartQuestionExample: the rock
1. ProblemWhat went wrong?After backing into the rock, the robot was crooked.
2. How we found outWhat did we test or measure?The next moves missed. We watched where it pointed.
3. What we changedWhat exactly did we change?We added face(0) right after the bump.
4. ResultWhat happened after? Give a number.It drives on straight. Works __ out of 10.
Weak: "We stopped doing that mission." That is not a fix.
Weak: "It broke, so we fixed it as a team." What broke? What did you change?
NOTES

ITERATE has a gear row: 'improvements based on testing'. A good fix story counts for Robot Design AND Core Values.

ITERATE · A WORKED EXAMPLE FROM THIS WEEK
The arm that was sometimes too high
StepWhat happened
ProblemThe arm in Phase 7 was too high on some runs and too low on others.
MeasureWe printed the motor's position after every move and logged every run.
FoundTwo runs started 45 degrees apart, though we thought they started the same.
Try 1Measure from the motor's own angle. Worked, until the attachment went back on.
Try 2Push the arm into its stopper to find zero. It lifted the attachment. Dropped.
FixThe stopper is zero. Good runs ended within 2 degrees, even after re-seating.
Still openA little play in the build. Next: a rubber band or bracing.
NOTES

Point out: two ideas failed, and that is fine. Judges score the process, not a perfect first try. Bring the printed log on the day.

ITERATE · ONLY ONE OF US GAVE A NUMBER
"It worked 8 out of 10" beats "it mostly works"
How to measure
1. Run the program 10 times, the same way each time.
2. Tally: worked, or didn't.
3. Write it in the run log with the date.
4. If you change something, do 10 more. Compare.
Why judges like it
A number proves we tested again and again. Before and after numbers prove the change helped.
 
Example: 6 out of 10, then we added face(0), then 9 out of 10.
NOTES

This is homework for whoever owns each run. Real numbers only. If we didn't measure it, we say so.
